%%bash -s "$PATTERN"
set -euo pipefail
# Retry transient network failures, then fail the cell instead of continuing without data.
retry() { for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do "$@" && return 0; echo "Attempt $i failed: $*" >&2; [ "$i" -lt 5 ] && sleep $((i * 15)); done; return 1; }
PATTERN=$1
[ -d ds000114 ] || retry datalad install https://github.com/OpenNeuroDatasets/ds000114.git
cd ds000114 && retry datalad get $PATTERN

children.value: The BIDSLayout instance is a lightweight container for all of the files in the BIDS project directory. It automatically detects any BIDS entities found in the file paths, and allows us to perform simple but relatively powerful queries over the file tree. By default, defined BIDS entities include things like “subject”, “session”, “run”, and “type”.

from bids.layout import BIDSLayout
layout = BIDSLayout("ds000114")

When a BIDSLayout is initialized, it scans and indexes all files and metadata within the specified root directory.  Once the indexing is complete, you can start exploring the dataset through different types of queries. The main method for this is
without any arguments, it simply returns a list of all BIDS files in the dataset:

all_files = layout.get()
print("There are {} files in the layout.".format(len(all_files)))
print("\nThe first 3 files are:")
all_files[:3]

children.value: Here’s how we would retrieve all BOLD runs with

# Retrieve filenames of all BOLD runs for subject 02
layout.get(subject='02', extension='nii.gz', suffix='bold', return_type='filename')
All the entities mentioned above are derived from the filenames in a BIDS dataset. However, sometimes we want to filter files not just by their names, but also using

defined in sidecar JSON files, as specified by the BIDS standard. When a BIDSLayout is initialized, it automatically indexes all associated metadata files. This means we can use any key found in a JSON file as a filter in
, and we can even combine these with core BIDS entities like subject, run, and task.

For example, suppose we want to retrieve all files that meet the following criteria:
(a) the RepetitionTime metadata value is 2.5,
(b) the task is either ‘covert_verb_generation’ or ‘finger_foot_lips’, and
(c) the subject is ‘01’ or ‘02’.
Here’s how we can do that:
objects by default. These are lightweight representations of individual files within a BIDS dataset and offer convenient access to various attributes and methods. Let’s explore what a
can do. To start, we’ll select a random file from the layout.

# Pick the 11th file in the dataset
bf = layout.get()[11]

# Print it
bf

provides a convenient interface to interact with individual files in a BIDS dataset. Depending on the file type, different attributes and methods are available. Keep in mind that some methods are only applicable to specific types of files—for example, you can’t use
Here are some commonly used attributes and methods:
– Name of the file (excluding the directory)
– Directory where the file is located
– Returns a dictionary of entities (e.g., subject, task) associated with the file; metadata can be optionally included
– Loads the file as a nibabel image (only valid for image files)
– Loads the file into a pandas DataFrame (works for .tsv files)
– Retrieves a dictionary of metadata from the related JSON sidecar(s)
– Lists other files that are linked to this one (e.g., JSON, events, or anatomical associations)

# Print all the entities associated with this file, and their values
bf.get_entities()

# Print all metadata of this file
bf.get_metadata()

# Get union of both of the above in one shot like this
bf.get_entities(metadata='all')

# Here are all the files associated with our target file in some way
bf.get_associations()
